How WinHelp Files Work
items.content:
I wanted Paperback to be able to open some old WinHelp files I had laying around, so I wrote libhlp, a pure-Rust reader for them. I had my wisdom teeth out on a Friday morning, spent the rest of that day completely out of it, and then woke up Saturday and did this instead of resting like a normal person. Recovering patients make great decisions.

Microsoft never documented the format, but Manfred Winterhoff did, in helpfile.txt, which ships alongside his decompiler, helpdeco. Between those and poking at real files, I worked out the format, and Claude wrote a lot of the actual Rust.

A file starts with the magic number , followed by the position of its internal directory. A help file is really an archive, and that directory lists the files inside it. Most of them have names starting with a pipe: holds the title and settings, holds the text, holds the fonts, holds the topic names, and pictures live in files like .

The directory is a B+ tree, and so is every other index in the file, all with the same page layout.

All the text lives in , which is cut into fixed-size blocks. Each block can be LZ77 compressed, and positions in the file count bytes of the decompressed text, not of the file itself. Every block also takes up the same amount of that address space whether it fills it or not. In a typical file, each block gets 16 KB of space and only decompresses to about 4 KB, so reading has to skip the gap to the next block.

Inside the blocks, the text is a linked list of records. Some records start a new topic, and the rest hold its paragraphs, each with a formatting part and a text part. The text part can be compressed a second time, which is where it gets fun.

Compression, part one: LZ77

WinHelp's LZ77 is about as simple as compression gets. The data comes in groups: one flag byte, then up to eight items. Each bit of the flag byte, lowest first, says whether its item is a literal byte or a back-reference. A back-reference is two bytes, with 12 bits of distance and 4 bits of length:

The length is stored minus 3, since anything shorter isn't worth a back-reference. A distance of 0 means "repeat the byte I just wrote", and since the copy can read bytes it's still writing, followed by a back-reference of length 5 becomes .

One fun quirk: some real files have back-references that reach behind the start of the data, where there's nothing to copy yet. helpdeco keeps its 4 KB window in a buffer that starts out full of zeroes, so those references just copy zeroes, and the files come out right that way. libhlp starts its window out zeroed too, instead of treating it as an error or reading off the front of the buffer.

Compression, part two: phrases

On top of LZ77, a help file can swap its most common phrases for short codes, and there are two versions of this.

WinHelp 3.1 keeps the table in . In the text, any byte from 1 to 15 starts a two-byte code, and every other byte is just itself:

The lowest bit of the code says whether a space follows the phrase. Phrases usually end at a word, so that saves a byte most of the time.

The Windows 95 help compiler added a fancier scheme, called Hall compression, with the phrases split across and . Here, the lowest bits of each byte say what kind of byte it is. If the lowest bit is clear, the rest of the byte picks one of the first 128 phrases, so the most common ones fit in a single byte. Ending in starts a two-byte code for the rest of the table, starts a run of literal bytes, means a run of spaces, and means a run of zero bytes. For the runs, the upper bits hold the length minus one, since a run of nothing would be a wasted byte.

doesn't store where each phrase starts. It stores how long each one is, packed into as few bits as it can get away with. Each length is a unary count in steps of some power of two, followed by the remaining low bits to add on top. The step size is set once for the whole file.

My first version always read at least one remainder bit. That works until a file uses a step of one, where there's no remainder to store. Then every length reads one bit too many, and everything after the first phrase is garbage. The fix was a single check.

When a help author wrote a topic, they gave it a context string, a name like . You'd expect a link to store the position of the topic it points to, but it actually stores a hash of the target's name. To follow a link, you hash its target name the way WinHelp does and look the result up in , which maps hashes to positions.

Each byte goes through a lookup table that gives uppercase and lowercase letters the same values, so links are case insensitive. The table's entries are signed, so anything at or above subtracts instead of adding. Get that wrong and almost every hash still comes out right, so it's really easy to miss. Oh, and an empty name hashes to 1, not 0, because that's what WinHelp does.

Text doesn't store its own formatting. A paragraph says "switch to font 4", and says font 4 is the bold one. Links are drawn the same way. WinHelp underlines a link by switching to an underlined font, so libhlp has to tell that underline apart from underlining the author actually asked for.

WinHelp is older than Unicode, so text is stored in whatever Windows code page the author used, which might be a double-byte one for East Asian languages. Sometimes the file's language ID says which one. When it doesn't and the text is mostly non-ASCII, libhlp guesses the code page from the text itself.

Then there's WinHelp 3.0, the version from Windows 3.0, which is different enough to almost be its own format. Its topic blocks are 2 KB and never compressed, its records give the distance to the next record instead of its position, its topic headers are 12 bytes instead of 28, and its links point at topic numbers instead of hashes. libhlp reads it, but it took its own commit.

And then there are the files that only share the extension. Borland's help compiler and MS-DOS QuickHelp both made files that have nothing else in common with WinHelp, so libhlp just turns those away.

It reads the text, titles, tables, emphasis, links and pictures of every WinHelp version I know of, from 3.0 to the Windows 95 compiler, and it bounds checks everything. Paperback uses it to open files, so if you've got an old one sitting around, now you can read it.

items.title: Sydney Fire Ant Infestation
items.content:
Authorities are ramping up efforts to manage a fire ant nest in Sydney after investigations revealed a larger and more complex infestation than first identified.

A nest detected in Auburn was successfully treated at the weekend, but further surveillance has revealed a more extensive presence of fire ants requiring intensive treatment and a broader biosecurity response.

It comes after Commonwealth authorities detected the insects, known for their painful sting, at the Enfield Intermodal Logistics Centre, in Sydney's inner west, on September 23.

Imported goods are suspected to be the source of both incursions, which are not otherwise believed to be connected.

NSW Agriculture Minister Tara Moriarty said a task force was being established to determine the ants' origins.

"The experts believe that they came in through containers that have come in likely from China," she said.

"At this stage, they are still only on this particular site in Auburn, but we will undertake further surveillance … to see if they have spread.

"I was able to check [the Auburn site] out myself yesterday, and even though the area is not geographically big, the types of ants that we have here do spread in a different way than what we've seen ants do in New South Wales."

Ms Moriarty said the Auburn infestation was located in an industrial area and included businesses that imported goods from Asia and elsewhere.

Management efforts underway

A biosecurity order is expected to be issued by Friday to regulate the movement of high-risk materials through Auburn, including soils, turf, mulch and building materials.

Additional biosecurity officers and detection dogs will also be deployed as part of the response.

Ms Moriarty said there had been more than 900 reports of suspicious nests from the public recent days, and asked locals to remain on the lookout for infestations.

"Biosecurity is everybody's responsibility,"

The ants are up to 6 millimetres long, dark reddish-brown with brown-black abdomens and are known to be aggressive.

Bites that have a burning sensation can cause itchy blisters or pustules and lead to the hospitalisation of children and death in severe cases.

If spotted, the nests must not be destroyed and members of the public are urged not to try to capture the ants, which are classified as prohibited matter in NSW.

Suspected fire ants can be reported to the Biosecurity Helpline on 1800 680 244.

items.title: What Is the Metabolism-First Theory for the Origin of Life?
items.content:
or well over 4 billion years, the fire of metabolism has powered the engines of life. The ability of cells to gather, transform, and harness chemical energy from their surroundings is the central force driving the dizzyingly complex network of chemical reactions that sustains living things.

Metabolism is so crucial to life that some researchers believe that these reactions could have helped spark life itself. They argue that life’s first glimmers were found in self-sustaining cycles of simple molecules, before genes or cells existed. Only later did more complex molecules like RNA and DNA develop and begin storing information for the purposes of heredity.

The core argument behind metabolism’s primacy is that without a self-sustaining reaction to provide energy, it’s impossible to explain how the larger and more complex molecules necessary for cellular life could have been produced at all. Energy going through the system is what life is in its many manifestations, said William Martin, an evolutionary biologist at Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf in Germany. “It synthesizes genes that contain the information to produce the catalysts that keep this reaction going, and those catalysts have changed over time.”

The concept that reactions driven by nonliving geochemistry could have eventually triggered living biochemistry has been decades in the making. In 1968, the American biophysicist Harold Morowitz proposed that energy that flows through a system organizes that system, and he applied this to the concept of a proto-metabolism. Essentially, Morowitz suggested that energy from external environmental sources, such as the sun or geologic processes, could nudge chemical networks into self-sustaining reactions because they were thermodynamically favored. In time, those could become biological reactions.

A very simple version of early self-sustaining reactions might be something like the acetyl-CoA pathway, a process that some modern microbes use to build complex organic molecules and generate chemical energy from hydrogen and carbon dioxide. But what conditions could have sparked these types of lifelike reactions?

Deep-sea submersibles first encountered hydrothermal vents in the late 1970s. These are wounds in the seafloor where geothermally heated water rich in dissolved metals pours out into the surrounding seawater. In the late 1980s and early 1990s, Günter Wächtershäuser, a patent lawyer with a doctorate in chemistry,  proposed the concept of an “iron-sulfur world.” In this possible early Earth environment, self-sustaining reactions like the acetyl-CoA pathway could have been chemically catalyzed by the iron-sulfide minerals collecting around these vents.

Here’s how that could have led to life. At first, a very simple pathway might have converted carbon dioxide and hydrogen into more complex carbon-containing compounds such as acetate and pyruvate, and released energy back into the environment. Hydrogen would have provided the energy; metallic catalysts kept this running in a loop. Once a primitive cycle was established, it could begin to produce increasingly complex compounds in layers, with more and more enzymatic loops, all gathering and releasing energy, building out from this original cycle. It’s possible that they could continue increasing in complexity well before any of life’s genetic mechanisms of inheritance had developed.

“You start out with a simple inorganic catalyst, and then organic catalysts, and then enzymes, and the metabolic process becomes more complex,” Martin said. “But the nature of the reactions that start without enzymes has been up in the air and hotly debated.”

To explore possible mechanisms, Martin and his colleagues mimicked temperature and pressure conditions around hydrothermal vents in the laboratory. In 2020, the team showed that chemicals found in these vents, such as carbon dioxide and hydrogen, along with nickel and iron minerals common at these sites, could combine to create formate, acetate, and pyruvate. These compounds are essentially the “spine” of the acetyl-CoA pathway, said Martina Preiner, a biochemist at the Max Planck Institute for Terrestrial Microbiology in Germany and lead author of the study. The findings “show that it’s possible to start these reactions before you have anything else,” including RNA or proteins, Preiner said.

However, some scientists argue that the heated and pressurized conditions around hydrothermal vents may not have been required to form these reactions. Also in 2020, Ramanarayanan Krishnamurthy, an organic chemist at Scripps Research in California, and his colleagues demonstrated that two small molecules that may have been present in an early Earth environment, pyruvate and glyoxylate, could react to form almost all the components of the reverse citric acid cycle — which is analogous to the acetyl-CoA cycle — and could do so not only at temperatures and in water conditions far removed from the more extreme environment of a vent, but also without any metal catalysts. This suggests that metabolism could have kicked off in a tepid pool rather than a deep-sea crucible.

Whatever environment provided the trigger, there is no well-formed understanding of how initial metabolic reactions could have become stable enough to develop complexity. Genetic material that can store and replicate information may have been necessary to transmit improvements to rudimentary metabolic reactions across generations.

Researchers also need to establish a connection between metabolism and genetic information, as well as determine how these proto-metabolic reactions might have coexisted without sabotaging each other once they were placed within the confines of cell membranes.

“How best can we mix them together so that we don’t get a complete mess that we can’t analyze?” Krishnamurthy said. “That is the challenge.”

Editor’s Note: Ramanarayanan Krishnamurthy has received funding from the Simons Foundation, which also funds this . Simons Foundation funding decisions have no influence on our coverage.

The Quantum Omelette Problem
items.content:
“Sunday or Monday, eat eggs every day.”

My mum took this advice rather seriously. On weekdays, we ate boiled eggs for breakfast. Sundays, however, were omelette days.

Our ritual was always the same. Each of us siblings announced how many eggs we wanted as we streamed into the kitchen. My mum cracked the eggs into a shiny steel bowl, added our chosen mix-ins, and whisked them together. The yolks, whites, salt, and chili powder quickly disappeared into one speckled mixture. She poured it into a hot, oiled pan, where it hissed and sizzled before sliding onto our plates.

The omelettes were soft, spicy, and gone within minutes.

My diet is now plant-based, but the nostalgia of those Sunday-morning breakfasts remains strong—the steel bowl, the sizzling pan, and all of us gathered around the table, waiting eagerly for the omelettes to arrive.

Our weekday boiled eggs and Sunday omelettes offer a useful contrast. In a boiled egg, the yolk and white remain distinguishable. In an omelette, they are mixed and transformed. Some properties—texture, flavor, and structure—belong to the finished mixture rather than to either component separately.

When two parts interact strongly, which properties still belong to the parts, and which belong only to the whole?

This question appears across science whenever interacting parts become difficult to describe independently. In quantum thermodynamics, it becomes a question of energy. Picture a small quantum system, an atom, say, surrounded by a much larger environment. The total energy of the setup comes from three sources: the atom, the environment, and their interaction.

When the atom barely interacts with its surroundings, separating the energy contributions is easy. The interaction energy is small enough to ignore, and we can speak cleanly of the atom’s energy and the environment’s. When the interaction is strong, however, that shared energy can no longer be brushed aside, making it difficult to decide how much belongs to the atom and how much to its surroundings.

For a large object, interactions with the environment typically occur at the surface, while most of its energy is associated with the much larger bulk. As an object grows, the surface becomes less important compared to its volume, so the interaction energy can often be ignored. But this reasoning breaks down for very small objects, where surface effects remain significant, or for systems whose interactions extend through the bulk, allowing interaction energy to scale with volume.

Such strong interactions are not limited to tiny systems; they also appear across condensed matter, nuclear, and high-energy physics. Lattice gauge theories provide one important example: their particles and fields are tied together by interactions and local constraints, making it especially difficult to draw a clean boundary around one part and declare, “This energy belongs here.”

In all these cases, the energy of the whole may be perfectly clear. The challenge, however, is deciding how to divide that energy among pieces that are no longer truly separate.

That brings us to a deceptively simple question: How should we define the internal energy of a strongly interacting system?

Definitions in physics do more than attach names to things. They tell us what counts as a system, which quantities can be measured, and how mathematical ideas connect to experiments. A useful definition must do more than sound reasonable: it should recover familiar results in familiar situations and remain consistent with the laws of physics. When two plausible definitions lead to different conclusions, the choice between them cannot be settled by language alone.

Consider the internal energy of a system. When a system is strongly coupled to its surroundings, some of the total energy is stored in the interaction, and several reasonable ways of assigning that shared energy become possible. But which definition of internal energy is consistent with thermodynamics? This is the question I explored with my collaborators Zohreh Davoudi, Christopher Jarzynski, Niklas Mueller, Connor Powers, and Nicole Yunger Halpern.

Physicists describe a system’s energy using a mathematical object called a . In our recent paper, we consider three ways of defining the internal energy of a strongly coupled system.

Definition 1: Subtract the environmentStart with the total energy of the system-environment composite, then subtract the energy the environment would have on its own at the same temperature. Whatever remains, including the interaction energy, is assigned to the system.

Definition 2: Include the environment’s influenceRather than separating the interaction energy by hand, describe the system’s energy using a that captures how the interaction energy affects the system’s energy at equilibrium. Physicists call this the Hamiltonian of mean force.

Definition 3: Account for temperature as wellThe Hamiltonian of mean force depends on temperature. The third definition takes this dependence into account when calculating the system’s internal energy.

All three definitions have appeared in the literature on strong-coupling thermodynamics, each offering a seemingly reasonable way to account for the environment’s influence on the system. We wanted to find out whether choosing one definition over another would change how we describe the same physical process.

To test the three definitions, my collaborators and I considered a —the physicist’s term for changing something in the setup almost instantaneously. Imagine rapidly turning a knob that controls the system, perhaps by suddenly switching on a magnetic field. We can also suddenly change how strongly the system interacts with its surroundings, effectively turning the interaction between them on or off. Either change happens so quickly that the system and its environment have no time to respond: their states remain constant during that instant. Yet the system’s internal energy can change because the rules governing it have changed. Since this energy change results from deliberate external control, we call it .

After the quench, the knob is left alone. The system then evolves under the new, fixed conditions and exchanges energy with its environment. This later change in the system’s internal energy is called .

Separating the process into two stages makes it easier to tell work and heat apart: work enters during the sudden, controlled change, while heat flows during the evolution that follows. It is a little like whisking an egg first and then placing it on a hot pan, rather than trying to whisk and cook it at the same time.

Once we have chosen a definition of a system’s internal energy, we can ask how that energy changes during any thermodynamic process. The first law of thermodynamics tells us that the change in internal energy must be accounted for by work and heat ,

The first law is essentially a statement of energy conservation. It tells us that any change in the system’s internal energy must be accounted for: the energy must have entered as work, as heat, or as some combination of the two.

But here is the catch. Each of the three definitions of internal energy comes with its own corresponding definitions of work and heat. If we change what we mean by , we also change how we split that energy change into and . For each of the three choices, however, the definitions are constructed so that work and heat add up to the total change in internal energy. All three therefore satisfy the first law.

At first, this seems reassuring. Perhaps any of the three definitions will do.

To decide whether all three internal energy definitions are truly acceptable, we need a stricter test: the second law. The first law tells us that energy must be conserved, but it does not tell us which direction a process will naturally take. The second law supplies that direction. An egg can be whisked and cooked into an omelette, but an omelette left on the plate will not spontaneously uncook itself, separate into a yolk and a white, and return to its shell. Energy conservation alone would not rule out such a reversal, yet nature overwhelmingly favors one direction. Cooking an omelette is therefore an irreversible process. A perfectly reversible process, by contrast, could be undone without leaving any lasting changes to the system or its surroundings.

For the sudden changes studied in the paper, we can quantify irreversibility by comparing the work actually performed with the minimum work required in an ideal, perfectly reversible process. Thermodynamics captures this minimum through a quantity called the free-energy change, ​. The difference between the actual work and this ideal minimum,

is called . It measures the extra work associated with carrying out the process irreversibly, and the second law says that it cannot be negative.

This is where the three definitions part ways. All three satisfy the first law, but only two satisfy the second law for the processes considered in the paper. The third definition, which accounts for the temperature dependence of the Hamiltonian of mean force, can predict negative dissipated work.

Does this mean that our quantum system has somehow broken the second law? Not at all. Rather, the third definition assigns internal energy, work, and heat in a way that makes a valid process look thermodynamically inconsistent.

The next question is why the three definitions agree in classical physics but separate in the quantum case. The answer lies in one of quantum mechanics’ defining features: observables do not always commute. Roughly speaking, when noncommuting observables describe two quantum properties, they cannot both be measured simultaneously. This has no direct counterpart in classical physics, where two observables describing different properties can be measured simultaneously. When the system’s energy and interaction energy cannot be simultaneously measured, the three definitions of work can give three different values.

To explore this connection, we considered what happens when the system’s Hamiltonian commutes with the interaction Hamiltonian, both before and after the sudden quench. In this classical-like limit, all three expressions for work give the same value, which also obeys the second law. In hindsight, the result may seem obvious. Still, there is something oddly satisfying about pinpointing precisely when the three definitions agree: strong coupling alone does not force them to give different answers. Quantum noncommutativity is what allows them to part ways.

Over the years, our family’s egg repertoire expanded. MasterChef episodes, new cookbooks, and travel brought poached eggs, Scotch eggs, shakshuka, eggs-in-purgatory, Tamagoyaki, and plenty of experiments in between. In some dishes, the yolk and white remain almost perfectly distinct; in others, the boundary between them nearly disappears. A whole spectrum exists between separation and complete mixing.

The same is true of a system and its environment: their interaction can range from barely noticeable to overwhelmingly strong. Our results identify two definitions that remain consistent with the laws of thermodynamics for the processes we studied, even when those interactions become strong.

Build your own amp modeler: $78 DIY pedal kit from TONE3000
items.content:
TONE3000 has sought to bring the biggest disruptor of today’s amp modeling game to the masses in a novel way by partnering with Daisy Audio for a DIY pedal kit.

This isn’t your standard build-it-yourself overdrive or fuzz pedal. Instead, this is a fully fledged capture and IR player that can be completely assembled at home, and tap into the ever-growing network of Neural Amp Modeler (NAM) tones.

It’s an enticing prospect. TONE3000 and the free-to-use NAM A2 have taken the gear world by storm this year, rewriting the rules of amp modeling in the process.

NAM A2 is widely believed to be one of the best modeling technologies of today, outperforming the industry’s big guns in a blind listening test. What’s more, it’s an open-source platform that lets players create, download and use captures of amps and effects for free.

Blackstar, Fractal, HeadRush, Positive Grid, Line 6 and Fender are all cottoning on to the game-changing tech – TONE3000 even launched a free plugin to play captures – but now NAM A2 hype has reached fever pitch with this new partnership.

According to TONE3000, every part of the pedal is open source, from the firmware and companion app to the schematic, circuit board, and drill template. In other words, anyone can build the pedal.

And it looks like a neat pedal, too. Once assembled, it has room for four presets, with a rotary switch to go between them. There’s a three-band EQ, as well as controls for Input, Output, and Noise Gate.

Once together, it can host any NAM A2 capture, of which there are quite literally hundreds of thousands. It can also stack captures, too, or run primary models into an Impulse Response.

Of course, this is way more advanced than wiring up an overdrive pedal, so the build is not for the faint of heart. TONE3000 goes as far as to suggest you should have at least two home builds under your belt before even thinking about this one.

It has about 150 solder joints, plus 14 wires to jacks, footswitch, and the rotary control. It has a through-hole construction, with no surface-mount parts. It’s all built on the Daisy Audio Seed3 module, which costs just $34.99.

The rest of the hardware comes separately courtesy of Tayda Electronics. That set is priced at $42.99, and comes with the circuit board, aluminum enclosure, and all the remaining bells and whistles. In all, that amounts to $77.98 for the entire pedal kit.

For those who aren’t afraid, the chassis has been made plenty big enough to inject a few modifications of your own.

“Daisy was built so anyone could turn an idea into a real piece of audio hardware,” says Daisy co-founder, Andrew Ikenberry.

“TONE3000 has taken state-of-the-art neural modeling and open-sourced every piece of the pedal around it, which is exactly the kind of project we hoped Daisy would make possible. We can't wait to see what builders do with it.”
